title: The Pilgrimage of Fulfillment
subtitle: Umrah al-Qada', the Peaceful Return to Makkah, and the Sacred Rites at the Kaaba
summary: In Dhu al-Qa'dah of the seventh year after the Hijrah, exactly one year after the pact at Hudaybiyyah, the Prophet and two thousand companions set out for Makkah to perform the promised lesser pilgrimage (Umrah al-Qada'). Chanting the Talbiyah as Quraysh evacuated to the surrounding hills, the Muslims circumambulated the Kaaba with dignified strength, performed the sacred rites in peace, and strictly honored the three-day treaty limit without incident.

sections.text: When the sacred month of Dhu al-Qa'dah arrived in the seventh year of the Hijrah, it brought the anniversary of the momentous Treaty of Hudaybiyyah. Under the terms stipulated in the treaty, the Muslims had agreed to withdraw that year without entering the sanctuary, on the express condition that they would be permitted to return the following year to perform Umrah unhindered for three days. With unwavering fidelity to treaties, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ summoned all those who had attended the Pledge of the Tree at Hudaybiyyah to prepare for the journey, accompanied by sixty sacrificial camels (al-hady).

Approximately two thousand believers donned the white garb of Ihram at Dhu al-Hulayfah, echoing the immortal declaration of monotheistic devotion through the desert canyons: 'Labbayka Allahumma Labbayk' (Here I am, O Allah, here I am). Mindful of Quraysh's past treachery, the Prophet dispatched an advance scouting party with sheathed defensive weapons stationed outside the sacred precinct at Marr al-Zahran, ensuring that the pilgrims entered the holy sanctuary of Makkah bearing only swords resting securely within their travel sheaths, exactly as agreed in the text of the treaty.

As the Muslim contingent approached the outskirts of Makkah, the leaders and clans of Quraysh, unable to bear the sight of their former exiles walking peacefully into their ancestral city, evacuated the valley floor and ascended the crests of Mount Abu Qubays and the surrounding summits to observe from above. Rumors had circulated among the pagan tribes that prolonged exile and the fevers of Yathrib (Madinah) had emaciated the believers and broken their physical spirit.

To refute these false assertions and project disciplined vigor before the observing idolaters, the Prophet instructed his companions to bare their right shoulders (idtiba') and to march briskly with purposeful, rhythmic strides (ramal) during the first three circuits around the Kaaba. In an authentic report recorded by Imam Muslim, the Prophet prayed: 'May Allah have mercy upon a person who shows them today strength in himself.'

أَمَرَهُمْ أَنْ يَرْمُلُوا ثَلاَثَةَ أَشْوَاطٍ، وَيَمْشُوا بَيْنَ الرُّكْنَيْنِ، لِيَرَى الْمُشْرِكُونَ جَلَدَهُمْ
'He commanded them to walk briskly for three circuits and to walk normally between the two corners, so that the polytheists would witness their endurance and strength.' (Sahih al-Bukhari 1602; Sahih Muslim 1266)
The Rites of Devotion and the Adhan of Bilal

The Prophet circumambulated the Kaaba upon his camel Al-Qaswa, touching the Black Stone and the Yemeni Corner with his staff, surrounded by companions who looked upon the Ancient House with tears of overwhelming gratitude. Abdullah ibn Rawahah walked in front of the Prophet, reciting poetry proclaiming the triumph of divine truth over falsehood. The Prophet gently guided him to recite words of remembrance and devotion rather than boasting.

Following the Tawaf and the two units of prayer behind Maqam Ibrahim, the Prophet proceeded to the hills of Safa and Marwah, completing the Sa'i with complete devotion. When the time for the noon prayer arrived, the Prophet commanded Bilal ibn Rabah—the formerly tortured Ethiopian slave—to ascend the roof of the Kaaba and proclaim the Adhan. Bilal's powerful, melodic voice resonated through every canyon of Makkah, proclaiming the greatness of Allah and the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ, striking deep into the hearts of the watching Quraysh.
Honoring the Treaty to the Final Hour

During his three days in Makkah, the Prophet concluded his marriage to Maymunah bint al-Harith al-Hilaliyyah, an alliance that further fostered goodwill and familial ties with prominent tribes of the region. When the morning of the fourth day dawned, marking the precise expiration of the seventy-two-hour allotment, representatives of Quraysh including Suhayl ibn Amr and Huwaytib ibn Abd al-Uzza came down and demanded: 'Your time has expired; depart from our land.'

Without a moment's hesitation or dispute, the Prophet ordered the entire Muslim encampment to strike their tents and depart immediately, fulfilling the treaty with immaculate honor. The Pilgrimage of Fulfillment proved to all Arabia that the Muslims were a disciplined, dignified community of profound spiritual gravitas and uncompromising integrity, paving the way for prominent Makkan leaders like Khalid ibn al-Walid and Amr ibn al-Aas to embrace Islam shortly thereafter.
